title: "L19 and L20: Statistical Inference"

```{r load-libraries, include=FALSE, message=F, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## The standard Normal distribution

- The standard Normal distribution $N(0,1)$ has $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$.
- $X \sim N(0,1)$ means the random variable $X$ is Normally distributed with that
  mean and standard deviation.

```{r std-normal, echo=T, warning=F, message=F, out.width="70%", fig.align='center'}
# You do NOT need to know this plotting code.
ggplot(data = data.frame(x = c(-3, 3)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), col = "orange") +
  labs(y = "density", x = "") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.46, label = "mean = 0 \nsd = 1", col = "orange") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.5)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, y = 0, xend = 0, yend = 0.4) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, y = 0, xend = 1, yend = 0.25, lty = 2) +
  annotate("segment", x = -1, y = 0, xend = -1, yend = 0.25, lty = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3,
                     labels = c(-3, "-2\n-2 SD", "-1\n-1 SD", "0\nmean",
                                "1\n+1 SD", "2\n+2 SD", 3))
```

Any Normal variable can be standardized with $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$. The
z-score is the number of standard deviations that $x$ sits above or below the mean.

## Confidence intervals for the mean $\mu$

The generic form of a confidence interval is

$$\bar{x} \pm z^* \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

$$\text{unbiased estimate} \pm \text{(critical value)} \times \text{(standard error)}$$

The critical value depends only on the confidence level you choose.

```{r critical-values}
# z* for the three common confidence levels.
# qnorm() gives the value with the stated area to its LEFT.
c(level_90 = qnorm(0.95),    # 5% in each tail
  level_95 = qnorm(0.975),   # 2.5% in each tail
  level_99 = qnorm(0.995))   # 0.5% in each tail
```

Note that higher confidence means a larger critical value, and therefore a wider
interval. You trade precision for confidence.

### Example on IQ scores (pg. 354)

We want the mean IQ score of seventh-grade girls in a Midwest school district.
Here are scores for 31 randomly selected girls. The standard deviation of IQ
scores is known to be 15 points.

```{r the-sample-data}
scores <- c(114, 100, 104, 89, 102, 91, 114, 114, 103, 105,
            108, 130, 120, 132, 111, 128, 118, 119, 86, 72,
            111, 103, 74, 112, 107, 103, 98, 96, 112, 112, 93)

iq_data <- data.frame(scores)

known_sigma <- 15
```

Three assumptions to check:

1. **Normality**. We can evaluate this with a histogram of the sample.
2. **SRS**. Only the description of the study can tell us this, not the data.
3. **Known $\sigma$**. Again, only the problem statement can tell us this.

```{r iq-histogram, warning=F, message=F, out.width="60%", fig.align='center'}
ggplot(iq_data, aes(x = scores)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, col = "white") +
  labs(x = "IQ score", y = "count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
```

The sample looks slightly left-skewed, but with only 31 observations a histogram
is lumpy even when the population really is Normal, so we proceed.

```{r calc-confidence-interval}
sample_mean    <- mean(scores)
standard_error <- known_sigma / sqrt(length(scores))
critical_value <- 1.96

lower_bound <- sample_mean - critical_value * standard_error
upper_bound <- sample_mean + critical_value * standard_error
```

```{r con_int2}
sample_mean
standard_error
lower_bound
upper_bound
```

Our best estimate of $\mu$ is 105.84, with a 95% confidence interval from 100.56
to 111.12.

**Interpretation.** If our model assumptions are correct and only random error is
affecting the estimate, this *method* for calculating confidence intervals will
contain the true value $\mu$ 95% of the time (19 times out of 20). Do not say
"we are 95% confident that $\mu$ is in this interval" — the 95% is a property of
the procedure, not of this one interval.

```{r ci-at-other-levels}
# The only thing that changes between confidence levels is the critical value.
sample_mean + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.95)  * standard_error   # 90% CI
sample_mean + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * standard_error   # 95% CI
sample_mean + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.995) * standard_error   # 99% CI
```

## Hypothesis testing, a one-sided example

Inorganic phosphorus in the blood varies among adults Normally with $\mu = 1.2$
mmol/l and $\sigma = 0.1$. A study measured 12 adults aged 75 to 79 to see
whether the level *decreases* with age.

```{r the-known-info-and-data}
phos <- c(1.26, 1.39, 1, 1, 1, 1,
          0.87, 1.23, 1.19, 1.29, 1.03, 1.18)

known_sigma <- 0.1   # sigma is given to us by the problem
```

$H_0: \mu = 1.2$ and $H_a: \mu < 1.2$. This is a **one-sided** hypothesis,
because the study asks only about a decrease.

```{r phos-mean}
mean(phos)
phos_data <- data.frame(phos)
```

```{r phos-histogram, out.width="60%", fig.align='center'}
ggplot(phos_data, aes(x = phos)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "forest green", col = "white") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(phos), col = "forest green") +
  annotate("text", x = mean(phos) - 0.04, y = 5.2, label = "Sample\nmean",
           col = "forest green") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.2, col = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.28, y = 5.2, label = "Null hypothesis\nmean", col = "blue") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(title = "Is the true underlying mean equal to 1.2?",
       x = "Phosphorus", y = "Count")
```

Assume $H_0$ is true. Then the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ for $n = 12$ is
Normal with mean 1.2 and standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

```{r phos-se}
n_phos <- length(phos)
se_phos <- known_sigma / sqrt(n_phos)
se_phos
```

```{r phos-null-dist, out.width="65%", fig.align='center'}
ggplot(data = data.frame(x = c(1.0, 1.4)), aes(x)) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 1.2, sd = 0.0289),
            fill = "#ec7014", xlim = c(1.0, 1.12)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 1.2, sd = 0.0289)) +
  labs(y = "density", x = "sample mean",
       title = "Sampling distribution under the null") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.2, lty = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.12, lty = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.06, y = 11, label = "observed\nsample\nmean")
```

The p-value is the shaded area, i.e. the probability of a sample mean this small
or smaller *if the null were true*.

```{r phos-pvalue}
pnorm(q = 1.12, mean = 1.2, sd = 0.0289)
```

About 0.28%, roughly 3 chances in 1000. That is strong evidence against $H_0$.

### The same test with a less extreme sample mean

Now suppose the sample had given $\bar{x} = 1.17$ instead. The hypotheses do not
change, because they come from the research question and not from the data.

```{r phos-pvalue-117}
pnorm(q = 1.17, mean = 1.2, sd = 0.0289)
```

About 15%, or roughly 1 sample in 7. These data give us no reason to doubt $H_0$.
Note carefully: this does **not** mean $H_0$ is true. We simply failed to find
evidence against it.

## Hypothesis testing, a two-sided example

Aspirin tablets are Normally distributed with a known standard deviation of 5 mg.
For an SRS of $n = 10$ pills we want to detect a mean that is different from
325 mg in *either* direction.

$$H_0: \mu = 325 \text{ mg} \qquad H_a: \mu \neq 325 \text{ mg}$$

```{r aspirin-setup}
mu_0        <- 325
sigma_pills <- 5
n_pills     <- 10
xbar_pills  <- 326.9

se_pills <- sigma_pills / sqrt(n_pills)
se_pills
```

```{r aspirin-two-sided, out.width="65%", fig.align='center'}
ggplot(data = data.frame(x = c(320, 330)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 325, sd = 1.581139)) +
  labs(y = "density", x = "sample mean",
       title = "A two-sided test has two shaded regions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 325, lty = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 326.9, lty = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 325 - (326.9 - 325), lty = 2) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 325, sd = 1.581139),
            fill = "#ec7014", xlim = c(320, 325 - (326.9 - 325))) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 325, sd = 1.581139),
            fill = "#ec7014", xlim = c(326.9, 330)) +
  annotate("text", x = 328.4, y = 0.13, label = "sample\nmean") +
  annotate("text", x = 323.8, y = 0.30, label = "null\nhypothesis") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.33))
```

```{r aspirin-pvalue}
# One tail. lower.tail = F because our sample mean is ABOVE the null value.
pnorm(q = 326.9, mean = 325, sd = 1.581139, lower.tail = F)

# Two-sided p-value: double it, because the Normal curve is symmetric.
pnorm(q = 326.9, mean = 325, sd = 1.581139, lower.tail = F) * 2
```

A p-value of about 0.23. If the true mean really were 325 mg, we would see a
sample this far off in one direction or the other about 23% of the time. That is
no evidence against $H_0$.

## The same calculation as a z test

Rather than working in the original units, we can standardize:

$$z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$$

```{r phos-z}
z_phos <- (mean(phos) - 1.2) / se_phos
z_phos
```

The sample mean sits about 2.77 standard errors below the null value.

```{r phos-z-pvalue}
pnorm(q = z_phos, mean = 0, sd = 1)
```

This is the same p-value we computed on the raw scale. (It differs in the fourth
decimal place only because the slides round the standard error to 0.0289, while
`se_phos` here keeps full precision.) Standardizing changed the labels on the
ruler, not the statistics.

```{r phos-z-dist, out.width="65%", fig.align='center'}
ggplot(data = data.frame(x = c(-3.5, 3.5)), aes(x)) +
  geom_area(stat = "function", fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1),
            fill = "#ec7014", xlim = c(-3.5, -2.768166)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, n = 101, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1)) +
  labs(y = "density", x = "z", title = "Same picture, now in standardized units") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -2.768166, lty = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.95, y = 0.33, label = "observed\nz-score")
```

### Choosing the right tail

| Alternative hypothesis | p-value | R code |
|------------------------|---------|--------|
| $\mu > \mu_0$          | $P(Z \geq z)$          | `pnorm(z, lower.tail = F)`     |
| $\mu < \mu_0$          | $P(Z \leq z)$          | `pnorm(z)`                     |
| $\mu \neq \mu_0$       | $2 \times P(Z \geq \lvert z \rvert)$ | `2 * pnorm(abs(z), lower.tail = F)` |

```{r all-three-tails}
z <- z_phos

pnorm(z, lower.tail = F)             # one-sided, greater than
pnorm(z)                             # one-sided, less than
2 * pnorm(abs(z), lower.tail = F)    # two-sided
```

Always sketch the curve and shade the region before writing the code. The picture
tells you which of these three lines you need.

## Confidence intervals and tests are two views of one calculation

A two-sided test at level $\alpha$ can be read straight off a confidence interval
with confidence level $C = 1 - \alpha$. If the null value falls outside the 95%
CI, the two-sided p-value is below 0.05.

```{r ci-and-test}
# The IQ interval from earlier was 100.56 to 111.12.
c(lower_bound, upper_bound)

# Is a null of mu = 113 inside that interval?
113 > lower_bound & 113 < upper_bound   # FALSE, so we would reject it

# Confirm with the test itself.
z_iq <- (sample_mean - 113) / standard_error
z_iq
2 * pnorm(abs(z_iq), lower.tail = F)    # two-sided p-value, below 0.05
```

The confidence interval is the better thing to report, because it also tells you
*how big* the difference plausibly is. A p-value alone throws that away.

## Check your understanding

A population is Normal with known $\sigma = 8$. You take an SRS of $n = 25$ and
observe $\bar{x} = 52$. You want to test $H_0: \mu = 50$ against
$H_a: \mu \neq 50$.

- What is the standard error?
- What is the z test statistic?
- What is the two-sided p-value, and what do you conclude at $\alpha = 0.05$?
- Does the 95% confidence interval contain 50? Does that agree with your test?

```{r check-understanding}
sigma_cu <- 8; n_cu <- 25; xbar_cu <- 52; mu0_cu <- 50

se_cu <- sigma_cu / sqrt(n_cu)          # 8 / 5 = 1.6
z_cu  <- (xbar_cu - mu0_cu) / se_cu     # 2 / 1.6 = 1.25
p_cu  <- 2 * pnorm(abs(z_cu), lower.tail = F)

c(standard_error = se_cu, z = z_cu, p_value = p_cu)

# The 95% CI. It contains 50, which matches p > 0.05: we fail to reject H0.
xbar_cu + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_cu
```
